A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TRiCo research work. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable. v2 retains Appendices A–G and adds Appendix H and a checklist.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments, component ablations, few-shot and distribution-shift evaluations, runtime measurements, and long-tailed classification results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds long-tailed and low-resolution evaluations, encoder comparisons, component-cost estimates, and further ablation and sensitivity results in Tables 20–25.

M1.justification: The frozen complementary encoders, two students, MI-based pseudo-label filtering, adversarial embedding generator, meta-learned teacher, losses, and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. Appendix H evaluates and further documents existing components without establishing a changed training procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix H substantially extends imbalance coverage beyond v1's CIFAR-100-LT evaluation: it reports CIFAR-10-LT and ImageNet-LT experiments and tabulates ImageNet-127 and low-resolution ImageNet-1k evaluations. CIFAR-10-LT is explicitly described as tested but has no separately identifiable result table. The CIFAR-100 encoder experiment changes the label setting within an already covered dataset.

E2.justification: Tables 20–21 add comparisons against FixMatch with ACR, SimPro, DARP, CReST+, and CoSSL, substantially expanding comparison with methods addressing imbalance. Table 23 also adds computational comparisons against MCT, whereas the retained Appendix B profiling compares against FixMatch. Existing comparator sets remain intact.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce many-shot versus tail-class accuracy reporting, 32×32 and 64×64 ImageNet evaluations, a 10%-labeled CIFAR-100 encoder comparison, and controlled sweeps of MI threshold, unsupervised weight, and perturbation budget. Table 21 explicitly evaluates ACR without anchor distributions. These extend evaluation design; the previously stated training protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H expands robustness analysis to additional imbalanced populations and resolutions, tests whether gains persist with weaker encoder pairs, and provides component-level computational analysis. Tables 24–25 add a consolidated component ablation, including a single-student control, and separate hyperparameter sensitivity sweeps. These extend the existing ablations, long-tail analysis, and failure analysis rather than merely relocating them.

E5.justification: v1 already reports three-seed standard deviations, bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired t-tests in Appendix C. v2 retains these and specifies five runs for Tables 22 and 24. However, H.2 claims five runs throughout while Section 3, Appendix C, and Table 20 retain three-run statements; the new checklist also incorrectly denies uncertainty reporting. A paper-wide increase in runs is therefore not established.

E6.justification: Tables 20–25 add substantial accuracy, overhead, ablation, and sensitivity results. Table 20 reports 68.1% tail-class accuracy for TRiCo versus 65.5% for FixMatch with SimPro; Table 21 also records a loss, 24.6% versus SimPro's 25.0% on 64×64 ImageNet-1k. Figure 1(a) changes plotted values, including roughly 96% to 95% for TRiCo at 4,000 labels, without explaining the revision. Tables 1–19 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The assumptions and Theorem 1 in Section 2.5, its proof in Appendix A, the complexity derivations in Appendix B, and the stopping-rule definitions in Appendix G are unchanged. Appendix H adds empirical analysis without new formal results or revised proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about triadic co-training, adaptive uncertainty-based supervision, robustness, low-label performance, and compatibility with frozen backbones. Appendix H supplies additional support without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: H.3 newly interprets gains across encoder pairs as independent of encoder strength and attributable to triadic co-training and MI regularization. H.4 interprets the sensitivity results as evidence of tuning robustness and the component costs as evidence of practical efficiency. These extend the interpretation of the unchanged method.

D1.justification: Table 23 adds implementation descriptions such as stop-gradient MI passes and operation on a single RTX 3090/A6000, alongside component resource estimates. The new checklist asserts an anonymized code release without supplying access instructions. These are additional disclosures; they do not establish replacement of the retained four-A100 experimental setup.

R1.justification: Appendix H extends comparative positioning toward specialized imbalance methods, explicitly discussing advantages over ACR and SimPro. The dedicated related-work section, the 47 referenced works, and the central novelty framing remain unchanged; bibliography differences concern citation-page references.

P1.justification: v2 appends Appendix H with five subsections and a NeurIPS checklist, revises the author and affiliation block, and removes the correspondence footnote. The existing scientific prose and section sequence are essentially unchanged, so this is an extension rather than extensive rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: Tables 20–25 substantially expand the empirical displays with class-specific results, resolution comparisons, encoder comparisons, component costs, ablations, and sensitivity grids. Figure 1 moves from page 2 to page 1, and panel (a) is redrawn with different colors, line widths, axis ticks, and vertical range. The other figure images and existing table structures are retained.

improvement.justification: Appendix H adds useful evidence addressing imbalance, dependence on encoder strength, computational cost, and tuning sensitivity. However, its global five-run claim conflicts with retained three-run descriptions, and the new checklist denies uncertainty estimates already present in v1. New benchmark protocols are sparsely specified, and Figure 1(a)'s numerical revisions are unexplained. The broader evidence and reduced reporting consistency create a tradeoff whose net effect on overall quality cannot be judged reliably.
